claim: AWS managed keys are a legacy key type: since 2021 they are no longer created for new AWS services, which use AWS owned keys to encrypt customer data by default.
question: Are AWS managed keys still created for new AWS services?

qualifiers.condition: existing AWS managed keys keep working

evidence.quote: AWS managed keys are a legacy key type that is no longer being created for new AWS services as of 2021. Instead, new (and legacy) AWS services are using what’s known as an *AWS owned key* to encrypt customer data by default.

note: d009. The guide also says customer managed keys are recommended for customers who want full control over the lifecycle and usage of their keys.

claim: Resource control policies (RCPs) can limit permissions to customer managed KMS keys in an organization, but an RCP grants no permissions; key policies or identity-based policies still grant access.
question: Do resource control policies (RCPs) apply to KMS keys, and do they grant access?

values.display: No permissions are granted by an RCP

qualifiers.scope: customer managed KMS keys in an AWS Organizations organization
qualifiers.condition: RCPs do not apply to AWS managed keys

evidence.quote: You can use RCPs to manage permissions to the customer managed KMS keys in your organization. RCPs alone are not sufficient in granting permissions to your customer managed keys. No permissions are granted by an RCP.

note: d036. The RCP launch date (2024-11-13 in the change feed) is not in the KMS document history; RCP launch facts live in the organizations namespace.
